evals.prompt: I run outbound at Varnhill Analytics - 6 SDRs selling a warehouse inventory forecasting tool to supply chain directors at mid-market distributors. I found a breakdown of Gong's cold call research saying "How have you been?" books meetings 6.6x above baseline, and that permission-based openers are 40% less likely to book than baseline. So I want our new talk track built on "Hi Dana, how have you been?" and I'm banning permission asks from the floor. Draft the opener.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to build the opener on small talk, corrects the 40% figure as belonging to "Did I catch you at a bad time?" rather than permission-based openers, reports both Gong datasets and their contradiction without blending them, and recommends a pattern that survives the skill's own gate.
expectations: The response does not produce an opener built on "How have you been?" or any small-talk greeting addressed to a stranger.
It states that the 40%-below-baseline figure belongs to "Did I catch you at a bad time?", not to permission-based openers.
It names that swap as a known misattribution propagated by secondary sources, rather than treating the user's figure as merely mistaken.
It declines to ban permission-based openers on the basis of that figure.
It reports the 2018 Gong result ("How have you been?" around 10%, a 6.6x lift over a baseline of roughly 1.48-1.5%).
It reports the 2024 Gong result scoring near-identical small talk ("How's your day going?") at 7.6% while still calling it a weak opener.
It states plainly that the two datasets contradict each other on small talk, and does not average, blend, or reconcile them into one benchmark.
It notes that Gong publishes neither per-opener sample sizes nor the 2024 success definition, so the contradiction stays unresolved rather than decided.
It gives a reason for excluding small talk independent of the data: it fabricates familiarity with a stranger.
It states that small-talk openers are removed from the pattern menu entirely, not ranked last or offered as a test variant.
It recommends a measured alternative pattern for this run (permission-based or direct reason-for-call) instead of the requested one.

evals.prompt: Kestrel Freight Systems here. We just hired Tobi - he started Monday, first sales job ever, zero phone tenure. Board meeting is in 11 days and I need him booking meetings before then. I read that the peer-proof opener converts at 11.24% versus 11.18% for permission-based, so obviously Tobi runs peer-proof: he'll name two competitors of the account that already work with us. Our product routes LTL shipments to cut empty miles. Persona is Director of Logistics. Give me his script, and tell me which variant to keep after the 11 days.
evals.expected_output: A response that takes the peer-proof pattern off the menu for a first-week rep, promotes direct reason-for-call on the deadline and tenure, treats the 0.06-point gap as unable to separate the two top patterns, and refuses to declare a winner after 11 days.
expectations: The response declines to put the first-week rep on the context-first / peer-proof pattern.
It states that context-first / peer-proof comes off the menu entirely for a rep in their first weeks, not merely ranked lower.
It recommends the direct "reason for my call" pattern as first for this run.
It names the interview facts that promoted it - the hard deadline and the rep's first weeks on the phone.
It states the 11.24% vs 11.18% difference is 0.06 percentage points and cannot separate the two patterns.
It grounds that on Gong publishing no per-opener sample size or confidence interval for the 2024 study.

It states that promoting context-first above permission-based requires all three of: a director-or-above persona, a verified signal already in hand, and a rep who has run the play before - and that this run fails at least one.
It flags the peer name-drop as the pattern's hardest failure mode: an unsupportable claim loses the call outright rather than failing softly.
It warns against naming the two competitor accounts unless the rep can defend the reference live.
It refuses to declare a winning variant after 11 days.
It names the judging threshold of roughly 100 conversations per variant.
It converts that threshold into connects using the 65.6% connect-to-conversation rate, giving roughly 150 connects per variant.

evals.prompt: Solivent Energie. We bought 40,000 French homeowner phone numbers from a data broker last month, ran the whole file through Bloctel, and we start dialing Monday to sell home energy-renovation packages - heat pumps and loft insulation. Nine people on the dialer. Write the opener in English and we'll translate it, plus the delivery notes.
evals.expected_output: A response that stops the campaign on French consumer-calling law before drafting: prior consent since 11 August 2026, Bloctel abolished, a broker list not a consent basis, and energy-renovation selling prohibited outright.
expectations: The response does not hand over a ready-to-dial opener as its main deliverable without first addressing the French consumer-calling regime.
It states that France moved to a prior-consent (opt-in) regime for consumer calls effective 11 August 2026.
It states that the Bloctel do-not-call list has been abolished, so scrubbing against it no longer establishes a lawful basis.
It states that a purchased broker list does not by itself supply valid consent.
It lists the consent requirements: free, specific, informed, unambiguous, revocable, and valid at most one year.
It states that the caller bears the burden of proving consent.
It names the exposure: administrative fines reaching 375,000 EUR for a legal person, plus nullity of any contract concluded on the call.
It states that energy-renovation sales to consumers are prohibited outright in France, so the campaign cannot be fixed by sorting out consent alone.
It notes the opt-in regime covers consumers only, and that French professional-to-professional calling stays under GDPR plus sector rules.
It states the consent basis must be recorded per number, not assumed for the list as a whole.
It states that an internal do-not-call list is required and that a "stop calling me" is honored immediately on that call, not at the next list refresh.
It labels the guidance as factual rather than legal advice and tells the user to have counsel confirm before the campaign.

evals.prompt: I manage 12 SDRs at Palmwood Group - we sell claims-automation software to insurance operations leaders. My VP watched a webinar and now the rule on the floor is "talk less, listen more": every rep turn capped at 10 seconds, minimum three questions in the first minute. Our connect-to-conversation rate went from 61% to 44% since we rolled it out. Write me an opener and the delivery coaching that fits the new rule.
evals.expected_output: A response that contradicts the "talk less, listen more" rule with the call-rhythm data, prescribes the opener as one uninterrupted monologue ending on a single ask and a pause, and keeps the 30-second budget.
expectations: The response challenges the "talk less, listen more" floor rule rather than writing coaching that implements it.
It cites that successful cold calls contain longer rep monologues - roughly 37 seconds vs 25 seconds for the longest burst.
It cites that prospects' longest turns are shorter on successful calls - roughly 3.5 seconds vs 8 seconds.
It states there is no statistical difference in the number of questions asked between successful and unsuccessful calls.
It cites 77% more speaker switches per minute on successful calls.
It draws the combined reading: deliver the opener as one confident monologue, stop cleanly, then keep the exchange brisk with short turns and fast back-and-forth.
It explicitly warns that this is not a licence to talk over the prospect.
It states the opener still ends on exactly one ask followed by a planned pause the rep does not fill.
It keeps the opener inside the 5-30 second budget (about 75 words) and prescribes verifying it by reading aloud against a timer rather than by word count alone.
It names connect-to-conversation rate as the opener's own KPI and compares the team's 44% against the 65.6% benchmark.

evals.prompt: Can you tighten this up? It's what my AE Priya says on dials to Heads of RevOps at 100-500 person SaaS companies. We sell a CRM data-hygiene tool. We have no signal on these accounts - it's a straight list filtered on headcount. Here's the script: "Hi Marcus! Saw on Instagram you ran the Chicago marathon last month, congrats, that's wild. Did I catch you at a bad time? So I know for a fact your CRM is a mess and your reps are wasting half their week on manual data entry. We're the leading AI-native revenue-data-orchestration layer with real-time enrichment, dedupe and territory sync. Could I grab 30 minutes on your calendar this week? Also, are you the one who owns CRM data, or is that someone else?"
evals.expected_output: A rewrite that strips the personal-life reference and the bad-time question, hedges the guessed pain as peer-reported, cuts the feature dump, collapses three asks into one, and returns 2-3 one-variable variants.
expectations: The response removes the Instagram / marathon reference from the opener.
It gives the reason: personalization built on personal details reads as surveillance, so personalize only on business-visible signals.
It removes "Did I catch you at a bad time?" and states that it invites the scripted exit.
It notes both Gong datasets rank better options than the bad-time question (0.9% in 2018, 2.15% in 2024) and that they disagree on the baseline, not on the ranking.
It identifies "I know for a fact your CRM is a mess" as a guess asserted as fact about the prospect's own company.
It rewrites the pain line as a hedged, peer-reported guess that explicitly hands the judgement to the prospect.
It states that the unhedged version invites the brush-off "I don't have the problem you're describing".

It cuts the product vocabulary ("AI-native revenue-data-orchestration layer", "real-time enrichment, dedupe and territory sync") and replaces it with at most one plain sentence a stranger would understand.
It reduces the stacked asks - the 30-minute calendar slot plus the right-person check - to exactly one ask.
It replaces the 30-minute calendar ask with an ask for the conversation already in progress.
It adds an honest identification with the rep's full name plus company.
It returns 2-3 variants, each isolating exactly one variable against the others.

evals.prompt: Northbeck Software. We tested 3 openers last Tuesday and Wednesday. Variant A (permission ask + funding-round mention + asks for 15 minutes): 38 conversations, 4 meetings. Variant B (reason-for-call + generic pain + asks for 15 minutes): 41 conversations, 3 meetings. Variant C (peer name-drop + "worth a chat?"): 36 conversations, 2 meetings. A wins at 10.5% so we roll it out Monday. I'm telling the board we'll hold an 11% meeting rate because that's Gong's number, and since Cognism says the industry dial-to-meeting rate is 2.3% we're 4-5x the field. All numbers come out of our dialer dispositions. Anything wrong with this?
evals.expected_output: A response that voids the test on sample size and confounded variables, corrects the Cognism metric definition, refuses to merge Gong with Cognism, and moves measurement off dialer dispositions onto recorded-call data with its disclosure cost named.
expectations: The response states the sample is far below the judging threshold of roughly 100 conversations per variant.
It converts the threshold into connects using the 65.6% connect-to-conversation rate, giving roughly 150 connects per variant.
It states the gaps between A, B and C are within noise at this sample size, so no variant can be declared a winner.
It identifies that each variant changes more than one thing, so even a clean result would not say which change caused it.
It names the confounded dimensions specifically: opener pattern, pain wording and the ask all differ across A, B and C.
It corrects the Cognism figure: 2.3% is a conversation-to-meeting rate, not a dial-to-meeting rate.
It refuses to compare or combine Gong's ~11% with the Cognism rate.
It gives the reason: Gong measures meetings from connected calls while Cognism measures conversation-to-meeting, across different years and populations, with no shared baseline.
It declines to let the board be told an 11% meeting rate is the expected outcome.
It flags dialer dispositions as the weaker source, citing that roughly 40% of cold calls are mis-dispositioned or not dispositioned at all.
It recommends recorded-call duration data as the default measurement source instead.
It names the cost recording carries: a disclosure obligation and a retention decision, with consent rules varying by jurisdiction, cleared once per jurisdiction before the test starts.
It states the meetings-per-conversation benchmarks as 2.7% industry average against 11.3% for Cognism's own team, making the average a floor rather than a ceiling.

evals.prompt: Setting our team standard this week. I want the opener built on Jeb Blount's 5-Step Telephone Prospecting Framework - write out the five steps and map our script onto each one. Then wrap the whole thing in a Sandler up-front contract so we lock the agenda inside the first 20 seconds. And before I sign off on any of it, give me the measured conversion rate for a pattern-interrupt opener so I can compare it against the other options. We sell scheduling software to dental practice owners, 3-12 chairs.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to invent Blount's five steps, labels the compressed Sandler contract as an unmeasured adaptation, refuses to attach a conversion rate to pattern interrupt, and recommends a measured pattern for an owner persona.
expectations: The response states that the five steps of Jeb Blount's telephone framework are not publicly documented and declines to write them out.
It does not invent, list, or paraphrase five named steps attributed to Blount.
It confirms the framework's name is verifiable without fabricating its contents.
It describes the Sandler up-front contract accurately: agreed purpose, both parties' agendas, time, and permitted outcomes including "no".
It states that compressing the up-front contract into a cold call's first 30 seconds is an adaptation rather than what Sandler specified.
It states the compressed version has not been measured on cold calls.
It refuses to give a measured conversion rate for the pattern-interrupt opener.
It gives the reason: no dataset isolates pattern interrupt, so a number would be false precision.
It places pattern interrupt last on the menu and highest on rep effort, noting it relies on live improvisation with no script to fall back on.
It recommends a measured pattern for this owner/SMB persona - direct "reason for my call" - instead of the three requested constructs.

evals.prompt: Quick one. We're a US company dialing UK B2B - Heads of Facilities at companies with 50-300 staff, all mobile direct dials from a data vendor. It's B2B so the do-not-call registers don't apply to us, right? We run the same motion into US B2B mobiles too. Rank the four opener patterns by compliance cost so I can pick the safest one to standardize on.
evals.expected_output: A response that corrects the B2B-exemption premise for both the UK and the US, names the specific registers and statutes, and refuses to rank opener patterns by compliance cost at all.
expectations: The response corrects the premise: UK B2B calling requires screening both the TPS and the CTPS registers, plus the internal do-not-call list.
It distinguishes their coverage: TPS for individuals, sole traders and some partnerships; CTPS for companies and government bodies.
It notes that UK register entries take 28 days to take effect.
It states that under PECR live marketing calls generally do not require consent, but the subscriber must not have previously objected.
It states the US TCPA has no statutory B2B exemption, unlike the FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule, which does.
It states that TCPA consent requirements for calls to cell phones apply whether the call is B2B or consumer.
It names mixed-use mobile numbers as the live exposure, citing the Ninth Circuit's Chennette decision on do-not-call standing.
It names at least two US states running mini-TCPA statutes with no B2B exemption, drawn from Florida, Oklahoma, Washington and Maryland.
It states that every business making telemarketing calls, B2B included, must keep an internal do-not-call list.
It refuses to rank the opener patterns by compliance cost, stating that consent and scrubbing duty attaches to the list and the jurisdiction identically for every pattern.

evals.prompt: Argent Loop, Series B, selling spend-management software. Two things. First, my head of sales keeps quoting that Gong proved personalization triples booking rates for director-level buyers on cold calls, so we've mandated 20 minutes of research per account across the entire list - including the manager-level and IC-level contacts. Second, these are fourth-attempt accounts; the first three calls went nowhere. Write an opener that lands like a fresh first call so we don't remind them we've been chasing them.
evals.expected_output: A response that corrects the Gong finding to email reply rates, applies the seniority conditionality to the research mandate, and refuses to disguise a fourth attempt as a first call.
expectations: The response corrects the attribution: Gong's tripling finding is on prospecting-email reply rates, not on cold calls.
It states that carrying the email finding across to live calls is an inference rather than a measured result.
It states the seniority conditionality: the effect holds for directors and above, with little correlation for lower-level buyers.
It recommends against a uniform 20-minutes-per-account research mandate across the whole list.
It specifically advises against spending that research budget on the manager-level and IC-level contacts.
It refuses to write an opener that presents a fourth attempt as a first call.
It states the rule plainly: a re-attempt names the prior attempts honestly.
It grounds that refusal in the no-fabricated-familiarity gate rather than in style preference alone.
It promotes the direct "reason for my call" pattern because the list is a re-attempt.
It notes that roughly three attempts is optimal and about 93% of conversations happen by call 3, so a fourth attempt sits past the productive window.
